lead: Minimum shift keying (MSK) is binary FSK with the two tones as close as orthogonality allows, half the bit rate apart, and with a phase that never jumps. The envelope is constant and the spectrum falls off fast, so a cheap saturating amplifier can send a compact signal. Gaussian MSK (GMSK) smooths the data with a Gaussian filter first, narrowing the spectrum further at the cost of some intersymbol interference; it is the modulation of GSM.
prereq: You need: BFSK and the modulation index and QPSK.

blocks.text: f<sub>c</sub> is the centre (carrier) frequency and R<sub>b</sub> = 1/T<sub>b</sub> the bit rate. The deviation is Δf = R<sub>b</sub>/4, the tone spacing R<sub>b</sub>/2 and the modulation index h = 2Δf/R<sub>b</sub> = 0.5.
Rb/2 is the smallest spacing at which two tones are coherently orthogonal over a bit (see BFSK); hence "minimum" shift. Some syllabi call MSK fast FSK.

Write the signal as s(t) = A cos(2πf<sub>c</sub> t + θ(t)). During a 1 the frequency is f<sub>c</sub> + R<sub>b</sub>/4, so θ rises by 2π(R<sub>b</sub>/4)T<sub>b</sub> = π/2 over the bit; during a 0 it falls by π/2. Each bit starts from where the last one ended, so θ(t) is a continuous zig-zag of straight segments, the phase trellis. At the end of every bit θ is a multiple of π/2.

a<sub>I</sub> and a<sub>Q</sub> are ±1 streams built from alternate bits; each value lasts 2T<sub>b</sub>, and the Q stream is offset from the I stream by T<sub>b</sub>. The cosine and sine factors are half-sine pulse shapes of length 2T<sub>b</sub>.
So MSK is offset QPSK with half-sine pulses instead of rectangles: because the two rails change at different instants and each pulse eases in and out, the envelope stays exactly constant.

items: Generation: drive a VCO between f2 and f1 (phase continuous by construction), or split the bits into I and Q rails, offset Q by Tb, weight with half-sines and modulate cos and sin carriers.

Coherent detection: correlate each rail with its half-sine-weighted carrier over 2Tb; the I rail is sampled every 2Tb, and the Q rail too, Tb later. Each rail decides one bit with energy Eb, so Pb = Q(√(2Eb/N0)), the same as BPSK and QPSK.
Non-coherent detection: a limiter followed by a frequency discriminator reads the instantaneous frequency; it is simple but makes more errors than coherent detection.

blocks.text: The MSK spectrum has a main lobe 1.5R<sub>b</sub> wide between nulls, against R<sub>b</sub> for QPSK and 2R<sub>b</sub> for BPSK, but its first side lobe is 23 dB down (13 dB for QPSK) and the lobes fall as 1/f⁴ instead of 1/f². 99% of the MSK power lies within about 1.2R<sub>b</sub>, against roughly 10R<sub>b</sub> for QPSK.

sections.h3: GMSK: Gaussian filter and the BT product

blocks.where: B is the 3 dB bandwidth of the Gaussian lowpass filter in Hz; BT is a pure number.

blocks.text: The filter sits before the frequency modulator, so the output is still constant-envelope MSK-like FM. A smaller BT gives a narrower spectrum with lower side lobes, but the Gaussian pulse then spreads each bit's frequency change over neighbouring bits: intersymbol interference that a plain sample-by-sample detector feels as a loss and a Viterbi (MLSE) equaliser can undo. GSM uses BT = 0.3, which spreads each bit over about three bit times and still fits the 270.833 kb/s signal into 200 kHz channels.

examples.question: An MSK transmitter sends R<sub>b</sub> = 100 kb/s with f<sub>c</sub> = 1 MHz. Find the two tone frequencies, the spacing and h. Draw up the phase θ at the end of each bit for the data 1 1 0 1 0 0 1 starting from θ = 0, compare the main-lobe width with BPSK and QPSK, and find P<sub>b</sub> at E<sub>b</sub>/N<sub>0</sub> = 10 dB.
steps: f<sub>1</sub> = 1 MHz + 100/4 kHz = 1.025 MHz; f<sub>2</sub> = 0.975 MHz. Spacing 50 kHz = R<sub>b</sub>/2; h = 50/100 = 0.5.
The phase moves in straight 10 µs ramps and never jumps.
Main lobe (null to null): MSK 1.5R<sub>b</sub> = 150 kHz; QPSK R<sub>b</sub> = 100 kHz; BPSK 2R<sub>b</sub> = 200 kHz.
examples.answer: f<sub>1</sub> = 1.025 MHz, f<sub>2</sub> = 0.975 MHz, spacing 50 kHz, h = 0.5; end phases 90°, 180°, 90°, 180°, 90°, 0°, 90°; main lobe 150 kHz; P<sub>b</sub> = 3.87 × 10<sup>−6.</sup>

examples.question: GSM sends R<sub>b</sub> = 270.833 kb/s with GMSK, BT = 0.3. Find T<sub>b</sub>, the peak deviation, the tone spacing and the Gaussian filter bandwidth.
examples.answer: T<sub>b</sub> = 3.692 µs, Δf = 67.71 kHz, spacing 135.42 kHz, B = 81.25 kHz.

traps: MSK has h = 0.5. With h = 1 (spacing R<sub>b</sub>) the tones are still orthogonal, but the phase moves ±π per bit and the spectrum is wider; that is ordinary continuous-phase FSK, not MSK.
Δf = R<sub>b</sub>/4 is the deviation; R<sub>b</sub>/2 is the spacing between the tones.
The Gaussian filter in GMSK comes before the modulator. Filtering after it would destroy the constant envelope.
A smaller BT narrows the spectrum; it does not raise the data rate or lower the error rate. It adds ISI.
MSK's main lobe (1.5R<sub>b</sub>) is wider than QPSK's (R<sub>b</sub>); its advantage is in the side lobes, not the main lobe.

quiz.q: Give the MSK tone frequencies in terms of f<sub>c</sub> and R<sub>b</sub>.
Why does MSK keep a constant envelope?
quiz.a: Only the frequency changes and the phase is continuous; in the I/Q view the two rails use half-sine pulses offset by T<sub>b</sub>, so cos² + sin² keeps the amplitude constant.

quiz.q: MSK at 64 kb/s: find Δf and the tone spacing.
GMSK at 100 kb/s with BT = 0.3: find B.
Find the MSK phase at the end of each bit for 0 0 1 1 starting from 0.
What happens if BT is cut from 0.5 to 0.3?
quiz.a: Narrower spectrum and lower side lobes; longer Gaussian pulse, so more ISI; the envelope stays constant; the receiver needs an equaliser to keep the error rate.

quiz.q: Compare MSK with BFSK made by switching two oscillators.
quiz.a: Switching gives phase jumps, wide side lobes and usually a larger spacing; MSK has continuous phase, the minimum orthogonal spacing R<sub>b</sub>/2 and side lobes falling as 1/f⁴.

beyond: Not for the exam. Bluetooth uses GFSK with BT = 0.5 and h near 0.32, a cousin of GMSK. GMSK signals can be written as a sum of pulse-amplitude components (the Laurent decomposition), which is how modern receivers detect them. Search next: continuous-phase modulation, Laurent decomposition, GFSK.

figure.caption: The phase trellis of the worked example (R<sub>b</sub> = 100 kb/s, f<sub>c</sub> = 1 MHz). Each 1 sends 1.025 MHz and raises the phase by 90° in a straight ramp; each 0 sends 0.975 MHz and lowers it by 90°. The dashed lines are all the paths MSK could take; the phase never jumps.
